positions/christian-physicalism/oneLine: Human beings are wholly physical organisms whose mental and spiritual capacities emerge from the complex functioning of the body and brain; there is no separable soul, and Christian hope is for the resurrection of the whole person.
positions/christian-physicalism/coreClai: Hebrew nephesh means a living being, not an immaterial soul.
Neuroscience shows that mind depends on brain at every level.
Higher capacities are real and not reducible to physics (non-reductive), but are not a separate substance.
Life after death is by resurrection, not natural immortality.
positions/christian-physicalism/origin: Developed in late-20th-century philosophy and theology by Nancey Murphy, Warren Brown, Joel Green, Peter van Inwagen and Kevin Corcoran; related to earlier “soul-sleep” and conditional-immortality traditions (Tyndale, Adventists).
positions/christian-physicalism/stronges: It fits Hebrew holistic anthropology better than Greek dualism.
It takes seriously the findings of neuroscience.
It places all Christian hope on bodily resurrection, as the New Testament does.
Dualists argue that it struggles to explain personal identity between death and resurrection (the “gap” problem).
Texts such as Luke 23:43, 2 Corinthians 5:8 and Philippians 1:23 imply conscious existence after death.
Critics argue it concedes too much to scientific naturalism and may undermine free will.
positions/christian-physicalism/response: Physicalists propose accounts of identity across the gap (God’s memory; constitution views; “immediate resurrection”).
They read intermediate-state texts as metaphorical or as compatible with soul-sleep.
positions/christian-physicalism/conseque: Renewed dialogue between theology and neuroscience.
Aligns with Adventist and conditional-immortality traditions.
positions/traducianism/oneLine: The soul, like the body, is transmitted from parents to children through natural generation, so that the whole person descends from Adam.
positions/traducianism/coreClaims/0: God finished creating on the sixth day; souls since then come through procreation.
positions/traducianism/coreClaims/2: It explains the inheritance of original sin without God creating sinful souls.
positions/traducianism/coreClaims/3: It treats the person as a unity of body and soul from conception.
positions/traducianism/origin: Taught by Tertullian (On the Soul, c.210); tempting to Augustine but never adopted by him; common among Lutherans (Formula of Concord context) and some Reformed (W. G. T. Shedd), and Eastern writers such as Gregory of Nyssa held related views.
positions/traducianism/strongestArgument: It explains both genetic resemblance and the transmission of original sin.
It avoids making God the creator of a soul that is immediately corrupt.
It fits Genesis 2:2 (God rested from creating).
positions/traducianism/strongestObjectio: Creationists of the soul object that a spiritual soul cannot be divided or generated by material processes.
Catholic teaching rejects it, holding that each soul is immediately created by God (Humani Generis 36).
Tertullian’s version made the soul corporeal.
positions/traducianism/responses/0: Traducianists answer that God works through secondary causes in generation, as in all providence.
positions/traducianism/responses/1: They insist transmission does not imply the soul is material.
positions/traducianism/consequences/0: Shaped Lutheran and some Reformed anthropology.
positions/traducianism/consequences/1: Supports realist accounts of original sin.
positions/soul-creationism/oneLine: Each human soul is created directly by God at conception (or ensoulment) and united to a body inherited from the parents.
positions/soul-creationism/coreClaims/0: The soul is spiritual and cannot be produced by material generation.
positions/soul-creationism/coreClaims/1: God is “Father of spirits” (Hebrews 12:9) who “forms the spirit of man within him” (Zechariah 12:1).
positions/soul-creationism/coreClaims/2: Each person is a direct work of God.
positions/soul-creationism/coreClaims/3: Original sin is transmitted through participation in Adam’s nature or by imputation, not by soul-generation.
positions/soul-creationism/origin: Defended by Jerome and Hilary against Origenist pre-existence and Tertullian’s traducianism; standard in medieval scholasticism (Lombard, Aquinas); Catholic doctrine (Humani Generis, 1950); held by Calvin and most Reformed.
positions/soul-creationism/strongestArgu: It safeguards the spirituality and dignity of each soul.
It allows Catholic teaching to accept bodily evolution while affirming that each soul is God’s direct gift.
It fits the biblical language of God forming each spirit.
positions/soul-creationism/strongestObje: Traducianists ask how God can create an innocent soul that is at once infected with original sin, or justly join it to a corrupt body.
It may suggest God creates souls continually, contradicting Genesis 2:2.
It struggles to explain inherited mental and moral traits.
positions/soul-creationism/responses/0: Creationists answer that original sin is the lack of original justice in Adam’s nature, which the new soul lacks because it is united to a body descended from Adam.
positions/soul-creationism/responses/1: Reformed creationists ground transmission in federal imputation, not physical descent.
positions/soul-creationism/consequences/: Became the Catholic and majority Reformed view.
Shapes debates over the timing of ensoulment in bioethics.
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/nam: Original sin as inherited guilt and corruption (Augustinian)
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/one: All humans were present in Adam and sinned in him, so that every human inherits both the guilt (reatus) of Adam’s sin and a corrupted nature marked by concupiscence; infants therefore need baptism for forgiveness.
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/cor: In Adam all sinned (Romans 5:12, read in the Latin in quo, “in whom”).
Humanity is a “mass of perdition” justly condemned.
Original sin is transmitted through generation, marked by disordered desire (concupiscence).
Baptism removes the guilt; concupiscence remains as weakness (Catholic) or as sin (Lutheran/Reformed).
Without grace humans cannot will the good.
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/ori: Developed by Augustine from 396 (To Simplician) and against Pelagius (412-430), building on Cyprian, Ambrose and Ambrosiaster; affirmed at Carthage (418), Orange (529) and Trent (1546), and in Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican confessions.
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/pro: Council of Trent, Decree on Original Sin (1546)
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/str: It explains the universality, depth and early onset of sin.
It undergirds the absolute necessity of grace and of Christ as second Adam.
It accounts for the ancient practice of infant baptism “for the remission of sins”.
Eastern Orthodox object that guilt is personal and cannot be inherited; Augustine’s reading of Romans 5:12 depended on a Latin mistranslation.
Pelagians and many moderns find it unjust that infants should be guilty for another’s act.
Evolutionary biology makes a single ancestral pair and a fall from original perfection hard to reconcile with human origins.
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/res: Augustinians respond that the doctrine rests on the whole of Romans 5 and on experience, not on one phrase.
They argue that humanity’s solidarity in Adam is the mirror of its solidarity in Christ; to deny one weakens the other.
Recent defenders reformulate it to fit human origins (Adam as representative or as head of a population).
positions/augustinian-original-guilt/con: Shaped Western sacramental practice, the theology of grace and the Reformation debates.
Influenced Western views of sexuality through the role of concupiscence.
positions/ancestral-sin-eastern/altNames: Greek patristic view of the fall
positions/ancestral-sin-eastern/oneLine: From Adam humanity inherits not personal guilt but a wounded nature subject to death and corruption; mortality and the fear of death drive humans into sin, from which Christ liberates by conquering death.
positions/ancestral-sin-eastern/coreClai: Guilt is personal; no one is guilty for Adam’s sin.
Adam’s fall introduced death, corruption and a disordered nature that all share.
Romans 5:12 should be read “because of which [death] all sinned” (eph’ hō).
Infants are baptised not to remove inherited guilt but to unite them to Christ’s life.
Salvation is healing and deification, not chiefly acquittal.
positions/ancestral-sin-eastern/origin: Rooted in Greek patristic exegesis (Irenaeus, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Maximus); articulated sharply against Augustinianism by John Romanides (1957) and John Meyendorff (1974); also characteristic of Oriental Orthodox and Church of the East teaching.
positions/ancestral-sin-eastern/stronges: It keeps guilt personal and so preserves divine justice.
It follows the Greek text of Romans 5:12 and the Greek Fathers.
It frames salvation as healing and victory over death, as in the Paschal troparion.
Western theologians respond that Romans 5:18-19 speaks of condemnation and of “many made sinners”, not just mortality.
Some Orthodox (e.g. Confession of Dositheus, 1672) used language close to inherited sin, so Romanides’ contrast may be overdrawn.
Critics argue it can underplay the gravity and bondage of sin.
positions/ancestral-sin-eastern/response: Orthodox reply that their view is no less serious about sin, since the corruption it describes is total apart from grace.
They argue that later Orthodox confessions borrowed Western categories under Latin and Protestant influence.
positions/ancestral-sin-eastern/conseque: Shapes Orthodox liturgy, baptism and the theology of theosis.
Became a focal point of Orthodox critique of the West in the 20th century.
positions/federal-headship/name: Federal headship and imputed sin (Reformed covenant theology)
positions/federal-headship/oneLine: Adam acted as the covenant (federal) representative of all humanity in a covenant of works; his first sin is legally imputed to all he represented, who therefore also inherit a corrupt nature — just as Christ’s righteousness is imputed to those he represents.
positions/federal-headship/coreClaims/0: God made a covenant of works with Adam as head of the human race.
positions/federal-headship/coreClaims/1: Adam’s guilt is imputed immediately to his posterity, prior to their own corruption.
positions/federal-headship/coreClaims/2: Corruption of nature follows as a penal consequence.
positions/federal-headship/coreClaims/3: The Adam–Christ parallel (Romans 5) requires representative headship.
positions/federal-headship/origin: Developed in Reformed covenant theology (Ursinus, Olevianus, c.1560s-80s; Cocceius 1648); confessed in the Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 6-7); defended by Turretin, Charles Hodge and much Presbyterian and Baptist theology.
positions/federal-headship/strongestArgu: It gives a clear, just rationale for universal condemnation that mirrors justification in Christ.
It does not depend on physical transmission or on a theory of the soul’s origin.
It coheres with the covenantal structure of the whole Bible.
positions/federal-headship/strongestObje: Critics argue that imputing guilt for an act one did not commit is a legal fiction and unjust.
Eastern and many modern theologians reject the covenant of works as absent from Genesis.
Union and Torrance theologians argue it makes God’s relation to humanity contractual rather than filial.
positions/federal-headship/responses/0: Federalists answer that representation is a common principle of justice and the very basis of salvation in Christ.
positions/federal-headship/responses/1: They point to Hosea 6:7 (“like Adam they transgressed the covenant”) and Paul’s Adam–Christ typology.
positions/federal-headship/consequences/: Structured Westminster and Puritan theology and the legal/forensic gospel framework.
Provides one evangelical option for reconciling a representative Adam with human origins.
